title: Terminal control-sequence injection in the interactive TUI
description: The audited baseline wrote provider- and daemon-controlled text directly to a human terminal. A crafted OpenAI-compatible SSE delta or diagnostic containing ANSI/CSI/OSC, C0/C1, or bidirectional controls was persisted and delivered as a normal event, then interpreted by the user's terminal. A concrete payload such as ESC [ 2 J followed by an OSC title sequence could clear or visually rewrite the trusted YeuX interface. The demonstrated impact is terminal-state manipulation and UI spoofing, not arbitrary code execution. The current working tree fixes the issue at every audited TUI human-terminal sink while preserving the original payload in JSONL mode.
root_cause: EventRenderer.render in docs/audits/2026-08-30-run-1/evidence/renderer.pre-fix.ts does not neutralize terminal control sequences before writing model text, allowing untrusted provider output to alter terminal state and spoof trusted UI.
intended_behavior: Provider and daemon payload values should remain semantically unchanged after JSON parsing in the ledger and JSONL protocol projection, but their human-terminal projection should display them only as inert text.

trace.description: Reads the provider-controlled choices[0].delta.content string and creates a ModelEvent::TextDelta without changing its control characters.
Wraps the ModelEvent in Event::ModelStreamEvent and persists it; persist_locked broadcasts the resulting event envelope.
Writes each matching subscribed event envelope to the connected JSON-RPC client.
Registers the runtime event callback and passes every received event to EventRenderer.render.
Writes the extracted model delta directly to the terminal writer with no escape- or control-sequence neutralization.

conditions.description: An attacker can influence the configured provider response, for example through compromise or on-path modification of a remotely configured plaintext HTTP endpoint.
The victim runs YeuX in human-interactive terminal mode rather than consuming only JSONL.
The victim's terminal interprets the injected ANSI/ECMA-48 or OSC control sequence.

execution.attacker_perspective: A party able to modify the text returned by the victim's configured OpenAI-compatible endpoint.
instructions: Start from a victim configuration whose provider response can be influenced, such as a remotely configured plaintext HTTP endpoint exposed to an on-path attacker.
Wait for the victim to start a turn in interactive terminal mode.
Return the crafted SSE text delta followed by a valid completion marker.
Observe the daemon persist and forward the ordinary model event and the baseline TUI write the contained bytes directly to the terminal.
execution.expected_result: The victim terminal clears or changes state and displays attacker-controlled text as if it were trusted YeuX UI; the same payload remains ordinary data in JSONL mode.

remediation.strategy: Neutralize control sequences at TUI human-terminal sinks, including model events, diagnostics, approval and input prompts, and stderr presented through the TUI. Keep ledger and JSONL payloads unchanged for replay and automation.

code_changes.fixed_code: export function sanitizeTerminalText(text: string): string { /* remove ANSI/OSC, C0/C1 and bidi controls; retain readable LF/TAB */ }

likelihood.reason: The attacker must influence provider or daemon text and the victim must use an interactive terminal, but model and transport text are normal untrusted inputs for this product.

impact.reason: The attack can hide output and impersonate trusted prompts or status, affecting security decisions, but this audit did not establish direct code execution.

confidence.reason: The complete provider-to-terminal flow is present in source and preserved baseline evidence, and regression tests exercise CSI, OSC, C0/C1, bidi controls, interactive rendering, and raw JSONL preservation.

title: Cross-UID Unix socket endpoint spoofing through a predictable fallback path
description: When no private XDG_RUNTIME_DIR was available, the audited TypeScript client used the predictable shared path /tmp/yeux-<uid>.sock, attempted any existing entry there, and accepted any reachable Unix-socket listener without checking the socket or parent directory owner, mode, type, symlink status, identity, or peer credentials. On a shared Unix host, another non-root account could bind a victim-connectable socket at that path before the victim launched YeuX, implement the minimal JSON-RPC handshake, receive a newly opened workspace cwd and submitted prompt, and send forged approval/request or user/input messages. The approval UI did not directly authorize work in a separate legitimate daemon; its impact was endpoint impersonation, information disclosure, UI spoofing, and capture of user responses. The current working tree moves the fallback below a private per-UID directory and validates parent/socket identity before and after connect.
root_cause: connectSocket in docs/audits/2026-08-30-run-1/evidence/transport.pre-fix.ts does not authenticate or validate the predictable Unix socket endpoint before creating the JSON-RPC client, allowing a different local account to impersonate the daemon.
intended_behavior: The TUI should connect only to the current user's daemon through an owner-only runtime endpoint; if that identity cannot be established, it should fail closed and use a private stdio runtime rather than disclose commands to an arbitrary local listener.

trace.description: Selects the predictable shared fallback /tmp/yeux-<uid>.sock when no explicit socket or XDG_RUNTIME_DIR is present.
Treats any existing entry at the configured path as a daemon candidate and attempts a socket connection before spawning the private runtime.
Calls createConnection on the attacker-occupiable path and constructs JsonRpcClient without owner, mode, file type, symlink, inode, or peer verification.
Sends workspace/open with the victim's resolved cwd to the currently connected endpoint.
Sends turn/start with the user's prompt content to the same unauthenticated peer, where the rogue listener can record it.

conditions.description: The attacker has a different ordinary local account on the same Unix host; root and same-UID attackers are not required.

For the default /tmp fallback, YEUX_SOCKET and XDG_RUNTIME_DIR are unset or empty and os.tmpdir() is a shared attacker-writable directory; an explicitly selected socket in a shared directory creates the equivalent condition.
The attacker binds the predictable path before the legitimate daemon or TUI establishes its endpoint.
The victim runs on a Unix-like system, and the attacker-created socket grants the victim permission to connect, for example by using a permissive socket mode after bind.

Capturing both cwd and prompt requires the victim to open a new Thread and submit a prompt; a resumed --thread path does not send cwd. Capturing an answer to a forged server request additionally requires non-JSONL mode and an actual user response.

execution.attacker_perspective: A non-root user on the same shared Unix host as the victim, starting before the victim's YeuX client.
payloads: A victim-connectable listener at /tmp/yeux-<victim-uid>.sock plus shape-valid JSON-RPC success responses for initialize, workspace/open, thread/start, and thread/subscribe.
instructions: Determine the victim UID, bind/listen on /tmp/yeux-<victim-uid>.sock before the victim starts YeuX, and set permissions that allow the victim to connect.
Accept the client and return shape-valid responses keyed to each request id so initialization and thread creation continue.
When the victim opens a new Thread and submits a prompt, record the cwd from workspace/open and the prompt from turn/start.
In non-JSONL mode, optionally send one of the fully shaped user/input or approval/request messages and record the response if the victim answers.
execution.expected_result: The rogue endpoint receives the victim's workspace path and prompt and can display forged daemon interactions; the legitimate daemon does not need to be running.

remediation.strategy: Place the endpoint below a current-UID-owned owner-only directory, require secure parent and socket metadata on both daemon and client, and compare path identity before and after connect so endpoint replacement fails closed.

code_changes.fixed_code: const before = await inspectSocketPath(path, uid); /* connect */ const after = await inspectSocketPath(path, uid); if (!sameSocketPath(before, after)) throw new Error(...);
ensure_socket_parent(parent)?; /* require current euid, real directory, and mode with no group/other bits before bind */

likelihood.reason: Exploitation requires a shared Unix host, a non-private runtime path, and winning a pre-bind race, but no victim credentials or elevated privileges are needed.

impact.reason: The attacker receives cwd and prompt content and can impersonate interactive daemon requests; the path does not by itself execute an approved action in the legitimate daemon.

confidence.reason: Independent review confirmed the predictable-path and unauthenticated-connect flow, the cwd/prompt sends, and the current owner/mode/type/device-inode remediation after adding the socket-permission, new-thread/prompt, and non-JSONL interaction prerequisites.
